name: Industrial brutalism
philosophy: Expose structure and assert a point of view while keeping controls predictable. Rawness is an art-direction choice; broken behavior is a defect.
influences: Utilitarian signage, printed work orders and early unadorned web structures supply visual cues. These are contemporary associations, not claims that all brutalist work has one origin.
characteristics: Visible borders and large typographic contrast
typography: Use one forceful display voice and an ordinary readable body. A monospace face can signal actual metadata; avoid turning paragraphs into a terminal. Let headings wrap instead of horizontally compressing letters.
color: Choose a strong ink/ground contrast and an accent tied to the subject. Bright signal colors can occupy broad areas. Check black or dark ink on bright fills before assuming white text is legible.
spacing: Tight internal alignments can sit within large structural gutters. Define border thickness and spacing roles; arbitrary cramped spacing does not make the design raw.
composition: An exposed grid, large project rows or purposeful collisions can create tension. Keep reading order and main navigation stable. Overlap only nonessential decoration or short display elements.
imagery: Use process documentation, workshop photographs or project artifacts. A rough crop can be intentional, but broken images and low-resolution product proof undermine credibility.
iconography: Simple directional or tool-like forms. Never rely on a custom symbol for an essential action without a label.
components: Square buttons, ruled lists and emphatic selected states. Preserve native form semantics; controls must remain distinguishable from bordered decoration.
interaction: Hover may invert colors or shift a small amount; keyboard focus needs its own state. All project rows must have meaningful destinations.
motion: Abrupt or stepped motion can fit the style. Prefer action feedback; stop recurring decorative motion on reduced-motion and provide pause for ongoing movement.
mobile: Replace layered desktop compositions with linear project rows. Keep the visual tension in type and border rhythm, not clipping or sideways scrolling.
accessibility: Strong contrast is helpful but not sufficient. Check landmark order, target spacing, focus visibility and whether all-caps passages are unnecessarily hard to read.
amateurish: Random borders, chaotic offsets and a hostile navigation system mistaken for intentional rebellion.
exceptional: The structure appears blunt yet every alignment, interaction and content transition has been resolved.
implementation: Use a small border token, semantic lists and grid rows. A 2px rule with no radius is a starting recipe, not a universal rule. Add :focus-visible independently of hover.
libraries: Native HTML/CSS is often the strongest base. A component library can provide behavior but should not dictate the visual container system.
evaluation: Is the primary task as discoverable as on a conventional layout?
Are apparently rough edges actually consistent?
Does the small-screen composition retain intent without overlap?
evidence: Original design recipe; source-linked engineering constraints. Not a validated causal model of visual quality.
